content: Bisphosphonate medications are commonly used to prevent and treat osteoporosis, as well as to alleviate symptoms and complications associated with metastatic bone disease. However, these drugs are linked to a rare but serious adverse effect known as bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (BRONJ). This condition is characterized by the presence of exposed bone in the maxillary or mandibular regions for more than eight weeks in individuals who are currently taking or have previously taken bisphosphonates, without a history of radiation therapy to the area. Currently, there is no universally accepted gold standard treatment for BRONJ. Treatment strategies can be broadly categorized into three groups: conservative approaches (such as the use of mouth rinses and antibiotics), surgical interventions, and adjuvant non-surgical therapies (such as hyperbaric oxygen therapy or platelet-rich plasma). These approaches may also be used in combination. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of various interventions for the treatment of BRONJ. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted up to December 15, 2015. These databases included the Cochrane Oral Health Group Trials Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others. Additional efforts were made to identify relevant studies by reviewing references, contacting experts, and searching clinical trial registries. Grey literature was also reviewed up to September 2015. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared the effects of any BRONJ treatment with another treatment or placebo. Two independent reviewers screened the search results, assessed the risk of bias in the included studies, and extracted data. Disagreements were resolved by consulting a third reviewer. Only one small RCT met the inclusion criteria, but it was determined to have a high risk of bias. This trial included 49 participants, most of whom had cancer. It compared standard care (defined as surgery, antibiotics, and oral rinses as determined by the oral-maxillofacial surgeon) with standard care plus hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBO). The HBO treatment involved exposure to 2 atmospheres of pressure twice daily for a total of 40 sessions. The trial assessed the percentage of participants who showed improvement or healing at three, six, 12, and 18 months, as well as at the last follow-up. Weekly pain scores were also recorded. At the three-month mark, participants in the HBO group were more likely to show improvement in their osteonecrosis compared to those receiving standard care alone (risk ratio [RR] 1.94, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.01 to 3.74). However, there was no significant difference between the groups in terms of complete healing at three months (RR 3.60, 95% CI 0.87 to 14.82). Similarly, no clear differences were observed between the groups for improvement or healing at six, 12, and 18 months, or at the last follow-up. The study did not report any data on adverse events. While the findings suggest that adjunctive HBO may improve BRONJ outcomes, the quality of the evidence is very low. This is due to several limitations of the study, including its small sample size, lack of blinding, crossover of participants between groups, and high attrition rates (50% at 12 months and 80% at 18 months, despite an intended follow-up period of 24 months). In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence from randomized controlled trials to guide the treatment of BRONJ. The single small trial evaluating HBO as an adjunct to standard care was unable to confirm or refute its effectiveness. Two ongoing trials are investigating the use of teriparatide for BRONJ, but no RCTs have been conducted for other treatment modalities. High-quality randomized controlled trials are urgently needed, and recommendations for their design and focus have been provided.
